title: Corsica
dek: Two women at Tomino in Cap Corse, and the reason this archive expects them to be strangers.
lead:
This archive holds **two people in Corsica**, and has never read a record for either. They are **Cattarina Defranceschi** and **Marie Jerome Defranceschi, born Bastiani**, both of **Tomino** in the Cap Corse, and both reached this project through the family tree rather than through a register.

Until today the site filed Corsica under *«not ours»*. That was **a guess wearing the clothes of a finding**, and it is corrected here. The honest position is stronger and more interesting than either a connection or a dismissal.

why.heading: Why this is a parallel and not a branch
why.text:
The surname is Italian. It is Italian in Istria and it is Italian in Corsica, and **that is the whole of what the two places have in common** — which is to say, nothing genealogical at all.

What they do share is a **shape**. Corsica was **Genoese** for four centuries. Genoa ceded it to France by the Treaty of Versailles in **May 1768**, and French control followed the fighting at **Ponte Novu in May 1769** — Napoleon was born at Ajaccio three months later, into a family that had been Italian subjects the year before. **Cap Corse**, the long northern finger where Tomino sits, was the most Genoese part of the island: it looked across at Liguria and Tuscany, traded wine and men with them, and its surnames are Ligurian and Tuscan.

So a *de Franceschi* at Tomino is almost certainly **an Italian family that became French by conquest** — exactly as a *De Franceschi* at Vodnjan became Austrian and then Croatian by treaty. **The same surname, caught by two different empires, four hundred miles apart.**

That is a real thing to write about, and it requires **no relationship whatsoever**. This archive expects these people to be strangers, and will say so unless a register says otherwise.

hold.close: **Zero records.** Not one search has ever been run in a French archive for this surname, by this project, in any commune. The Corsican material is the least-worked ground the archive has, and it is also — unusually — the ground with the **best records**.

route.heading: Where the records are, and they are unusually good
route.text:
Corsica is better served than Istria. The **Archives départementales de la Haute-Corse** at Bastia digitised its civil registration in 2008–2009 — **797,814 pages** — and the *état civil* of **all** communes, **1793 to 1902**, is online and free. The first tranche, Aghione to Pigna, went up in 2010 and the remainder followed; **Tomino is covered.**

Two warnings before anyone gets excited. The online set is chiefly the **greffe** collection — the clerk's duplicate — and it is **very incomplete for the earliest revolutionary years**; in most communes the series effectively begins around **year XI**, that is 1802–03. And **1793 is a floor, not a bottom**: everything before it is *parish* register, kept separately, and Cap Corse's pre-revolutionary books are a different search in a different place.

**None of this is FamilySearch**, which matters today: it is not blocked, it needs no login, and it can be worked while Vodnjan is refused.

plan.heading: How this archive intends to work it
rows: **Tomino first, exhaustively.** It is a tiny commune. Read the whole *état civil* for the surname across 1793–1902 and take **every** hit, not only the two names already held.
**Then the Cap Corse communes around it** — Rogliano, Ersa, Macinaggio and their neighbours. A surname in Cap Corse will sit in a cluster of villages, not one.

**Then the parish registers before 1793**, which is where the question of a Ligurian or Tuscan origin is actually settled — and where any *real* comparison with the Istrian story would have to be made.

**Prove nothing.** Every Corsican person entered gets the line **corsica**, and the page will keep saying *parallel, not branch* until a document says otherwise. The two women stay marked **tree, unverified** until a register names them.

open.heading: What is open
rows: Whether Tomino is one family or several
Two women of the surname in one tiny commune may be a household or a coincidence. **Nothing yet says which.**
Where the Corsican Franceschi came from
Liguria and Tuscany are the obvious candidates, and Cap Corse's whole history points that way — but *obvious* is not *documented*, and this archive has been wrong about obvious before.
Whether the Napoleonic officers belong here at all
Our own Namesakes page carries two Frenchmen of the name. They are recorded because they exist, **not because they are relatives**, and that has not changed.
Switzerland and Savoie, still untouched

Four **DeFranceschi** graves at Giubiasco in **Ticino**, and one **Pierre Defranceschi** at Gaillard in **Haute-Savoie**, which is effectively a suburb of Geneva. Both look like modern Italian labour migration and neither has been searched. **They are two more separate stories, not part of this one.**

source: People from the family's MyHeritage tree and from gravestone records; not one has been confirmed against a register. Historical background: the Treaty of Versailles of 15 May 1768, Ponte Novu, May 1769, and the Genoese administration of Cap Corse. Record availability from the Archives départementales de la Haute-Corse, whose civil registration for 1793–1902 was digitised in 2008–2009 and published for all communes.
